content:
Hollywood's most famous underdog finally gets his own underdog movie. I Play Rocky, Peter Farrelly's drama about how a broke, unknown Sylvester Stallone fought to write and star in Rocky, opens in select theaters today, Friday, November 6 — with a nationwide expansion set for November 20, timed to the original film's 50th anniversary season. The film also opens in cinemas in the United Kingdom today.

Anthony Ippolito stars as the young Stallone, with AnnaSophia Robb as his partner Sasha Czack, Matt Dillon as his father Frank Stallone Sr., Stephan James as Carl Weathers, and Tracy Letts in a supporting role. The film is written by Peter Gamble and directed by Farrelly, the filmmaker behind the Best Picture winner Green Book. Amazon MGM Studios is releasing it, and it runs 127 minutes.

The story it tells is one of the best-known legends in Hollywood. Inspired by journeyman boxer Chuck Wepner's 1975 bout against Muhammad Ali, Stallone wrote the Rocky screenplay in about three and a half days, then turned down big-money offers from studios that wanted anyone but him in the lead. He held out until he could play Rocky Balboa himself.

The gamble paid off beyond anyone's imagination. Rocky was made for roughly $1 million and shot in just 28 days, then won the Academy Award for Best Picture and earned Stallone an Oscar nomination for his screenplay. The original film, released November 21, 1976, turns 50 this month and is returning to cinemas in a re-release.

Critics are welcoming the new film warmly. I Play Rocky holds an 88 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes from 78 reviews, climbing roughly 20 points since its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September. Reviewers have singled out Ippolito's performance — the actor previously played a young Al Pacino in The Offer — with Cinemalogue's Todd Jorgenson calling it "a lighthearted tale of artistic inspiration and creative ingenuity, the film is elevated by Ippolito's scrappy performance that transcends mere mimicry."

Not every review is a knockout. Some critics note the film softens parts of the historical record and gives Apollo Creed limited screen time. But the opening-day consensus is that Farrelly has delivered a crowd-pleaser, and one that could put Ippolito on the awards-season map the same way Rocky did for Stallone.

Analysis: Why this opening matters beyond the nostalgia

Rocky is not just a movie; it is Hollywood's founding myth about betting on yourself, and I Play Rocky works because the story behind the film is the same story the film tells. Stallone's refusal to sell his script without the starring role is the rare case of an artist's stubbornness becoming the entire point of the work. Fifty years on, with the original returning to theaters and a new film retelling its making, the franchise's legacy is being measured not in sequels and spinoffs but in the idea that launched it: an unknown actor who would not take no for an answer.
